Eat
ēt
v.t. (rendering Hebrew 'akal, Greek esthiō/trogō)
From Saxon etan, to eat, cognate with Latin edo and Greek edō. Hebrew 'akal is used of men, of beasts, of fire consuming, and of the sword devouring — the one verb covering nourishment and destruction, since to eat a thing is to make an end of it and to make it part of oneself.

Biblical Definition

The history of the race turns twice on a meal. The first fall is described in the plainest possible verbs: “the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes... she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat” (Genesis 3:6) — the whole ruin of Adam's posterity carried on an act of eating against a word of God. The recovery is announced in the same register, and it scandalised the crowd: “Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you” (John 6:53). What the Lord requires there is not a physical mastication but a real receiving of Himself — faith doing with Christ what teeth do with bread, taking Him wholly in until He becomes the life of the man. Between the fall and the feast the ordinary meal remains a moral act. The passover was eaten standing and ready to march: “thus shall ye eat it; with your loins girded, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand” (Exodus 12:11). And Paul makes work the condition of bread in an ordered church: “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Nothing in Scripture treats eating as a neutral animal function. It is obedience or rebellion, communion or gluttony, and the table is where a man's religion becomes visible.

Webster 1828 Definition

To take food into the stomach; to consume; to devour. In Scripture, Eve took of the fruit and did eat; the passover eaten in haste with loins girded; Christ's command to eat His flesh and drink His blood; and the rule that he who will not work shall not eat.

expand to see more

EAT, v.t. 1. To bite or chew and swallow, as food; to masticate and swallow for nourishment.

2. To corrode; to wear away; to consume, as fire or rust.

3. To enjoy; to partake of; as, to eat bread with a man, denoting fellowship.

4. From Saxon etan; Latin edo; Greek edo. The primary sense is to take in, to consume.

5. In Scripture, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, Gen. 3; except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, John 6.

Key Scripture

Genesis 3:6 — "And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, and gave also unto her husband with her; and he did eat."

John 6:53 — "Then Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you."

2 Thessalonians 3:10 — "For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat."

1 Corinthians 10:31 — "Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God."

Modern Corruption

John 6 is pressed into a doctrine of physical eating, so that the Supper is made to convey Christ by digestion rather than by faith; and at the other pole, the table is stripped of moral weight altogether and eating treated as a matter beneath religion.

expand to see more

Rome takes the eating of John 6:53 as literal mastication and finds transubstantiation in it: the substance of the bread becomes the body of Christ, which is then eaten by the mouth, so that grace is conveyed by the act performed. Lutheran sacramental union softens the mechanism but keeps the oral eating. The Lord Himself forecloses the reading in the same discourse: “It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life” (John 6:63), and He identifies the eating with coming and believing in verse 35. The Reformed confession keeps everything the text says and refuses what it does not: Christ is truly received in the Supper, spiritually and really, by faith, so that the believer feeds on Him — while the unbeliever chews bread and receives judgment.

The opposite corruption is the modern indifference that treats appetite as an amoral appetite. Scripture does not agree. It names gluttony among the sins, sets a table before the believer as the highest picture of communion with God, makes the Supper the church's central act, and closes the canon with a marriage supper. Paul's rule — whether ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God — refuses the division of life into sacred acts and neutral ones. The principle to recover is that a man who cannot govern his eating has not yet learned that his body is not his own; and a church that eats together without discerning the Lord's body eats to its own harm.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'akal, to eat, consume, devour; lecheem, bread or food, that which is eaten; Greek esthiō, to eat, and trōgō, to chew or gnaw, used in John 6.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'akal (H398) — to eat, devour, consume; used alike of men at table, fire on a sacrifice, and the sword in battle.

Hebrew 'okel (H400) — food, that which is eaten; the noun of Genesis 3:6, the tree good for food.

Greek esthiō (G2068) — to eat; the ordinary verb, used of the passover and of the Lord's Supper.

Greek trōgō (G5176) — to gnaw or chew audibly; the deliberately physical verb of John 6:54-58, pressing the reality of the receiving.

Greek koinōnia (G2842) — communion, fellowship; the word Paul uses of the cup and the bread in 1 Corinthians 10:16.

Usage

"Of the first transgression: she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat (Genesis 3:6)."

"Of receiving Christ by faith: Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man... ye have no life in you (John 6:53)."

"Of ordered diligence in the church: if any would not work, neither should he eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10)."
